principles.text: Let new positions get stopped out if they trigger the stop — no second-guessing and no ego; don't try to prove yourself right when the market tells you you're not.
When price is already below your stop, waiting and hoping generally leads to a larger loss — take the exit.
Don't panic-sell all positions or initiate shorts on a gap-down day; a gap down into support is a bad place to flip bearish.
Weigh the full index picture before turning bearish — it is hard to justify a bearish stance while IWM is still trending steadily above its 9 EMA even if SPY looks ugly.
On reversal days when the market is below the 9/21 EMA you can simply sit out and wait for confirmation — a 60-minute reclaim of the 9 EMA, or the daily 9/21 breakout — before buying.
Red-open days that bounce intraday are the best days to spot relative strength — the stocks holding green while the market is down are the likely leaders of the next leg up.
Anticipation entries below the declining 9/21 EMA have a higher chance of failure, so offset the low win rate by risking a tiny amount (e.g., 0.1-0.15% of portfolio) with a very tight stop.
Have no P&L goals — focus on your trades only; P&L is a byproduct, and if you take good care of your trades the money will follow.
Avoid moving stops to break-even as a habit — either take the planned loss or let the position do its own thing.

Let the entry location dictate the exit style: a buy off the lows / a pullback into the 50 EMA is a solid consolidation worth holding through with the stop, while a buy off the 9 EMA or near highs should lean toward selling more into strength because a deeper pullback (to the 21/50 EMA) is more likely.
For a breakout volume signal to matter it should be truly parabolic in dollar terms — roughly double prior days or a step-change in daily dollar volume — not just modestly elevated.
When the market is mixed and direction is unclear, be patient and let the market tell you — pick one bellwether stock (his 'anchor') to monitor as the read on market strength.
